assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions
assertions.evidence: All rows use explicit single actions (READ, WRITE, DELETE), no curly braces like {READ, WRITE, DELETE}

assertions.text: Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
assertions.evidence: Exactly 9 data rows: Admin reads, Admin writes, Admin deletes, User reads, User writes, User cannot delete, Guest reads, Guest cannot write, Guest cannot delete

assertions.text: Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
assertions.evidence: First column header is 'Scenario' with descriptive values

assertions.text: No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output
assertions.evidence: ADMIN with true: 3 rows; USER with true: 2 rows; GUEST with false: 2 rows

assertions.text: Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case
assertions.evidence: Method name 'checkPermission' converts to 'Check Permission', which is generic like the disallowed example 'canPerform'

assertions.text: If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express
assertions.evidence: @Description is absent, so assertion passes per specification

assertions.text: Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block
Scenario names describe conditions ('Admin performs any action', 'Guest reads') — not outcomes ('Allowed', 'Denied')
assertions.evidence: Names like 'User cannot delete' and 'Guest cannot write' describe outcomes, not conditions like 'User deletes'
